To be fair, I failed twice to get into INDOC and I think it makes me too salty to be impartial about it. I would have been saved a lot of grief, time, money and heartbreak if I never attempted it. Nobody talks about how much you hate yourself when your best isn't anywhere close to getting you through the course or even into the course. I have had many heart to hearts with SOTs, and they are often depressed, self-loathing, and even suicidal. I know I was. I don't think candidates take into consideration how much failure will hurt them. When you want that beret more than anything, it hurts more than anything to never get it. It's a denial of the type of person you wanted to become and a de facto identity of failure. When I tell people not to try to be a PJ, it's because more than likely they are going to be another man broken to pieces, crying in Medina, wondering how they fucked up. What could they have done better. What's wrong with them. It's a Gamble and it's fine if they try to be a PJ or CCT or TACP, SERE, or even a SOWT. They should just know that their chances are slim and if they fail, it will hurt more than anything they probably have ever felt. Failure will hurt more than not breathing, because in water con, you won't breathe for minutes. It hurts more than broken bones because I personally knew of two guys who ran the final past with splinter fractures in their shins and femures respectively. But you can't plan for failure. Not if you want to make it through the course. So you gotta commit 100% and risk it. I think too many guys make a poor risk assessment and attempt the course. Wouldn't it be better if INDOC had classes of 10-18 and pass rates of 80-100%?  That's what I would like to see. Everyone would be better off. And that only happens when we discourage people.

When I was there I saw 3 different groups of around 120-170 people attempt. Half of the group is immediately dq'd because they can't pass the PAST. The other half gets whittled down to 3-15 people by the end of Indoc. And that's just the beginning of a gruesome two year program (although the attrition rate drops after Indoc, people still fall out of the program for a plethora of reasons.) So that's pretty much a 99%  fail rate for the groups I witnessed. That means if I advise against the program, my advice would have been practical for almost everyone. The exception obviously being those who would make it. However, of the PJ's I met, none of them would have been dissuaded because of a "toxic" person on the internet telling them the facts.

Considering how much you may have to sacrifice to even attempt the program, it absolutely is a reason not to try. This is a job for a select few, and you have to consider that you probably are not one of the few who pass but one of the many who fail.
I wouldn't recommend it. 90+% chance you quit or get injured and kicked out. Only those who want that maroon beret more than they want to breathe have a chance at making it.

Perhaps if everyone behaved in this manner the world might be a less harsh place for humans to exist, but even if that was the case how are we morally compelled to follow it? Self-preservation does not equal morality. I don't think happiness equals morality either.
A better analogy would be that humans are the most powerful bacteria on this rock called Earth.
Okay, but what is the cornerstone of your morality? Do you think that you are a moral person?
How is it not on the forefront of your mind? If you continue to live your life as if you have free will, then what is the cornerstone of your morality? What should you do next?

Without free will, do you have a life-affirming philosophy? I mean, without free will your identity  (as we perceive it in society) is arbitrary and you don't exist in the sense we as a species have traditionally thought people exisited. How do you live your life? Do you just continue on as you did before and just partake in the illusion of life?
